Highest eval latency (0.2783 ms) and second-lowest speedup (0.355); fp32 4096x4096 provides the 2x-bytes contrast against t7

performance_interpretation: Round 1 is a PASSED eval (geo_mean 0.4911, 30/30 workloads) but a total profiler loss: five msprof collections covering four timing workloads, three dtypes, two element-count extremes (1024 and 16.7M) and both advertised levels all returned the identical 'msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker', with zero artifacts, empty metrics and capabilities [] every time. No manifest was accepted as a downloadable artifact, so this analysis carries no profiler findings at all; the only measured numbers available are the eval latencies returned by get_profile_context, and they are used here strictly as arithmetic, never as counters. Two workload-scoped regimes are visible from those latencies. (a) The nine timing workloads with N<=1048576 form one launch/overhead regime: 16.5-19.4 us nearly independent of element count across all three dtypes (fp16 17.95 / 17.04 / 19.25 us at N=1024 / 65536 / 1048576; fp32 16.92 / 17.11 / 19.24 us), while the reference sits on a comparable 12.4-14.5 us floor, so the 2.6-4.7 us gap there is roughly constant additive overhead rather than a per-element cost, and the headroom for host-side work is bounded by that floor. (b) The three 4096x4096 workloads are a separate regime whose latency is dtype-invariant to within 4.7% (0.2690 fp16 / 0.2715 bf16 / 0.2783 fp32 ms) even though fp32 moves 2x the bytes in both directions, whereas the reference is strongly dtype-dependent (0.03145 / 0.01915 / 0.09888 ms). That signature is consistent with the frozen hypothesis that the ~20-26 FP32 vector ops per element in _round_value are the limiting resource, since the kernel converts every element to FP32 and then runs an identical op sequence for all three input dtypes; it is inconsistent with these three cases being limited by MTE2/MTE3 byte volume. It is not proof: AIV versus MTE active ratios, per-program UB occupancy, spill or serialized sub-tile processing, block-count efficiency and the device-task-versus-full-call split asked for in questions 1-3 all remain unmeasured. The geometric mean is dominated by these three cases, so the only change worth spending a round on is one that cuts per-element FP32 vector work; the block-size question is deliberately left alone because the 1024x element-count sweep shows walltime is flat where op count per element is constant.

next_experiment.action_description: In _round_value, replace the floor/fraction/int32-parity/3x-tl.where RNE sequence with the single magic-constant RNE on the already-computed magnitude: rounded = (magnitude + 8388608.0) - 8388608.0, reusing the existing 'magnitude >= 8388608.0 -> magnitude' passthrough select that is already in the code. That add/sub pair is an exact round-to-nearest-even-to-integer for |x| < 2^23 because the FP32 add itself performs RNE at ulp=1 in [2^23,2^24). Then delete the now-redundant NaN/Inf guard: NaN makes the magnitude compare false and falls through the passthrough select, and Inf takes the passthrough branch, so 'where((xf != xf) | (abs(xf) == inf), xf, signed)' is subsumed. Keep the explicit sign-bit re-application (and 0x80000000 / or) because the magic path returns +0.0 for small negative inputs and round(-0.4) must be -0.0. Keep the DECIMALS != 0 scale multiply and tl.div_rn tail unchanged, and keep abs() in front of the add because the trick only holds for non-negative values. Expected op count per element drops from roughly 26 to roughly 10-11 (cvt in, abs, add, sub, cmp, select, bitcast-and, bitcast-and, or, bitcast, cvt out), and live FP32 temporaries drop by about 5, which also relieves any UB pressure at block=4096.
next_experiment.expected_impact: The three 4096x4096 workloads are the geometric mean's whole problem (speedups 0.117 / 0.0705 / 0.355 against 0.64-0.85 for the other nine). If their latency tracks FP32 vector-op count, a ~2.4x op reduction should pull 0.269-0.278 ms toward roughly 0.11-0.15 ms, moving t3/t7/t11 speedups to about 0.21-0.29 / 0.13-0.17 / 0.66-0.90. With the nine small workloads unchanged near 17 us, that alone lifts geo_mean from 0.4911 to roughly 0.60-0.66. If instead the large cases move less than about 15%, the compute-bound hypothesis is falsified and the next round should look at UB pressure and access granularity rather than arithmetic.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Correctness risks, all testable on the existing 18 correctness workloads: (1) the magic add/sub pair must not be reassociated or folded by the compiler; verify numerically and, if needed, break the pair with a non-foldable barrier rather than accepting silently wrong results. (2) The -0.0 sign is the known trap for this operator family (a sibling pointwise operator in this batch passed its contract while emitting +0 instead of -0): the sign-bit OR must be kept, and round(-0.4) / round(-0.5) must be checked explicitly since the contract only requires matched_ratio 1.0 under atol/rtol. (3) Strided inputs must keep going through _round_strided with identical numerics: the change is inside _round_value so both paths inherit it, but re-run the strided cases. (4) NaN handling changes from an explicit select to falling through the magnitude compare; confirm equal_nan behaviour and that inf/-inf survive both the passthrough select and the sign-bit or. (5) bf16 inputs can exceed 2^23, so the passthrough select at exactly 8388608.0 is load-bearing and must not be widened or narrowed. (6) The decimals != 0 path keeps div_rn, so the threshold stays relative to the scaled value as it does today. Rollback: the change is confined to the body of _round_value, so reverting to the current formula restores the measured 0.4911 baseline exactly; hold the current main.py as the fallback artefact before editing.
success_criteria: Formal KGS eval reports status PASSED with all 30 workloads passing (18 correctness including strided and special-value cases, 12 timing), matched_ratio 1.0 and no new tolerance or runtime failures.
round_out-timing-7 latency drops below 0.15 ms (speedup > 0.13 from 0.0705), t3 below 0.15 ms (from 0.2690) and t11 below 0.16 ms (from 0.2783).
Headline geo_mean rises from 0.4911 to at least 0.60; treat 0.55-0.60 as a partial win and below 0.55 as falsification of the compute-op-count hypothesis.
No timing workload regresses: the nine small workloads stay at or below about 0.020 ms each, and no speedup among them falls below its round-1 value by more than 5%.

warnings: Profiler collection failed 5/5 times; status is failed rather than inconclusive because no artifact of any kind was produced, and the record system accepted no manifest as a downloadable artifact. No pipeline utilization, MTE2/MTE3 activity, UB occupancy, block-count efficiency, spill data or instruction listing exists for round 1, so no finding below is backed by a counter.

dominant_bound=mixed is inferred from eval latency shapes only: launch/overhead for N<=1048576 and vector-instruction count for N=16.7M. It is not backed by any profiler counter and should be treated as a hypothesis.

The candidate's contiguous path uses the cached low-level launcher compiled.run.launch(...) with packed metadata. That entry point bypasses the normal Triton launch wrapper, and the source itself checks launcher.enable_msprof_register_tensor as a reason to refuse the fast path. Whether the fast path is what breaks msprof base collection is untested: every timing workload shares the same path, so no non-fast-path timing workload exists to compare against.

Project guidance for a missing msprof completion marker is respected: no hardware instruction, pipeline or occupancy fact is derived from source or TTIR here. Source-derived statements are limited to launch geometry and launch-path structure.
The eval is PASSED and geo_mean 0.4911 is the authoritative headline; nothing in this analysis revises it.
open_questions: Question 1 unanswered: for t3/t7/t11 the split between AIV vector-issue and MTE2/MTE3 movement is unmeasured; only the eval-level byte-invariance argument rules out bandwidth dominance.

Question 2 unanswered: device-task duration versus full-call duration was never separated, so the exact host dispatch share of the ~17 us small-input floor is unknown; only the upper bound (the whole 16.5-19.4 us) is established.

Question 3 unanswered: no UB occupancy, spill or serialized sub-tile evidence was produced, so whether block=4096 (16 KiB per FP32 intermediate, roughly 10-12 live temporaries in _round_value) is UB-pressured cannot be confirmed. Grid is 4096 programs at N=16.7M, 256 at N=1048576, 16 at N=65536 and 4 at N=1024 over a 20-AI-core device, so N=65536 leaves 4 cores idle, yet eval latency shows this did not matter (0.0170 vs 0.0179 ms).

Question 4: the frozen hypothesis (~20-26 vector ops per element drive the large-case gap) is neither confirmed nor contradicted by profiler evidence; it is only found consistent with eval-level dtype invariance. The recommended experiment is designed to falsify it.

Profiler retry guidance: all five attempts died at the same base-collection stage regardless of workload, dtype, size or level, so the defect is environmental or launch-path related rather than workload related. A cheap next probe is to take one round without the cached compiled.run.launch fast path so the standard _round_flat[grid] entry is used and then re-request metrics; this is a hypothesis about the collection failure, not a finding.
No repeat profiling was possible, so every latency quoted here is a single-eval value with unknown repeat spread.
